results.title: GPU rental prices are rising in 2026 — the dated evidence | GPUJournal
highlights:
### The verdict

- Nebius — Raised rates across the board. H100 SXM now $4.50/hr.
- RunPod Secure — Raised Secure Cloud rates. H200 $4.59 → $5.29/hr (▲ 15%); RTX 4090 $0.74 → $0.89/hr (▲ 20%).
- Verda — Three rises in four days — all nine rose on Oct 23 and Oct 26; seven of nine rose again on Oct 24. H100 SXM $4.34 → $4.61/hr (▲ 6.2%).
- The cheapest offers — No movement in our records. The best verified H100 offer is still $2.25/hr.

## The evidence, date by date

Every rise below was read on the provider's own published pricing page on both sides of the change — the before figure and the after figure, each with its date. That is the standard our Price Watch applies to every entry. October 1 — Nebius raises across the board: Nebius lifted its on-demand rates at the start of October, and our board carries the post-rise rates (H100 $4.50/hr, H200 $5.40/hr, B200 $8.50/hr, verified Oct 19 and re-read unchanged Oct 26). October 14 — RunPod Secure goes up: RTX 4090 rose from $0.74 to $0.89/hr (▲ 20%) and H200 from $4.59 to $5.29/hr (▲ 15%) on RunPod's Secure Cloud; both rates were re-read on RunPod's own page on Oct 24 and Oct 26 — unchanged since the rise. October 23, 24 and 26 — Verda rises three times in four days: all nine Verda GPUs rose on Oct 23 and again on Oct 26, and seven of the nine rose on Oct 24 as well (A100 40GB and L40S held that day) — the full table is below. We are not the only ones seeing it: a third-party analysis published Oct 21, 2026 found H100 prices up at six of seven specialist GPU clouds during 2026. Our own records cover October in daily detail; the direction agrees.

### Verda — three rises in four days, in full

All figures USD per GPU per hour, read on verda.com/pricing on each date shown.

| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| H100 SXM | $4.34 | $4.51 | $4.56 | $4.61 | ▲ 6.2% |
| H200 | $5.66 | $5.89 | $5.95 | $6.01 | ▲ 6.2% |
| B200 | $8.07 | $8.36 | $8.44 | $8.52 | ▲ 5.6% |
| B300 | $10.28 | $10.69 | $10.80 | $10.91 | ▲ 6.1% |
| GB300 | $11.82 | $12.29 | $12.42 | $12.55 | ▲ 6.2% |
| A100 80GB | $2.07 | $2.13 | $2.15 | $2.16 | ▲ 4.3% |
| A100 40GB | $1.52 | $1.56 | $1.56 | $1.58 | ▲ 3.9% |
| RTX PRO 6000 | $2.40 | $2.49 | $2.52 | $2.54 | ▲ 5.8% |
| L40S | $1.77 | $1.81 | $1.81 | $1.83 | ▲ 3.4% |

### The half that has not moved

Against those rises, the cheapest verified offers on our board did not move at all during the week of Oct 19–26:

| GPU | Best verified offer | Provider | Oct 19 → Oct 26 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| H100 SXM | $2.25/hr | TensorDock (8-GPU minimum) | — unchanged |
| H200 | $3.59/hr | RunPod Community | — unchanged |
| B200 | $5.98/hr | RunPod Community | — unchanged |
| RTX 4090 | $0.20/hr | nafnaf | — unchanged |
| A100 80GB | $1.09/hr | Thunder Compute | — unchanged |

Read the terms before you chase the floor — minimum commitments and community-cloud availability differ from list-rate clouds. But the fact stands: on Oct 26 you could still rent an H100 for roughly half the rate a rising list price asks ($2.25 vs $4.50–$4.61). Rising list prices have not pulled the floor up — yet.

...

GPUJournal reads providers' own published pricing pages and banks the figures at every check. The checks behind this page fell on Oct 19, 22, 23, 24 and 26, 2026 — there are gaps between them, so the October rises are documented check by check rather than day by day. A price change we catch in our own checks is only reported when both the before and after figures were seen on the provider's own page, each with its date; that is how the Verda and RunPod rises above were verified. The Nebius rise of Oct 1, 2026 is different: it predates our records and was an announced rise, so we did not bank both sides of it ourselves — we verified the post-rise rates on Nebius's own page (checked Oct 19, re-read unchanged Oct 26) and report it as announced. And a price a provider merely states about itself never appears on our board as a verified price. Where a provider's pages state figures we cannot verify, Price Watch reports them labelled as stated — which is how disagreements get exposed rather than hidden: on Oct 26, Spheron's pages stated the same H100 at $2.64 on some pages and $2.98 on others, and we report the disagreement rather than pick a number.

results.title: Nebius raises GPU list prices up to 21% while H100 spot sits at $0.79 - CTOL Digital Solutions
highlights:
Posted prices for four Nebius GPU types rose 17 to 21 percent on 1 October. Its own spot board shows Blackwell chips near 60 percent of list and an H100 at the floor, so the squeeze sits in particular chips and regions.

Nebius told CNBC this week that AI computing prices are rising faster than it expected. On 1 October it lifted the posted price of four GPU types by 17 to 21 percent. Anyone renting GPUs has to decide whether that posted price is what they will pay.

...

### What changed in the price list

The Nebius pricing documentation dates two changes. The first took effect on 1 October, when on demand prices per GPU hour rose for four chips. Reuters reported on 17 September that Nebius had announced it, its second price rise in three months.

- B300 went from $7.85 to $9.50, up 21.0 percent, the largest rise.
- B200 went from $7.15 to $8.50, up 18.9 percent.
- H200 went from $4.50 to $5.40, up 20.0 percent.
- H100 went from $3.85 to $4.50, up 16.9 percent, the smallest rise of the four.

The RTX PRO 6000 stayed at $1.80, so the rise did not reach every GPU.

The second change came on 8 October. The preemptible tier, which rents interruptible capacity at a discount, stopped using fixed prices. It moved to dynamic spot pricing that can change every 15 minutes.

One rule in the documentation matters most. The highest spot price is always one cent below the current on demand rate, so the new list price is a ceiling. The floor is $0.79 or $0.99 depending on the chip. The posted price rise matters to a spot buyer only when the market pushes against that ceiling.

...

On 21 October Nebius announced public live spot pricing, also shown on Shadeform, Silicon Data and GPU Finder. Nebius's spot board shows how far below the ceiling each chip sits. At 23:03 UTC on Wednesday, B300 cleared at $5.29 to $5.89 across three regions, 56 to 62 percent of list.

...

Across five Blackwell regions, then, spot cleared at 52 to 62 percent of list. That is 38 to 48 percent below the posted price, well

...

Crusoe's on demand H200 and H100 sit below Nebius's list. Its pricing page lists on demand H200 at $4.29 an hour, 21 percent under Nebius's posted price. H100 is $3.90, and B300 is $9.90 against $9.50 at Nebius.

results.title: Four pricing changes in eight days at one provider. None at another. | Compute Stacker
results.author: Compute Stacker
highlights:
Four pricing changes in eight days at one provider. None at another.

What actually happened on H100 rate cards this month:

- October 1: Nebius raised on-demand H100 from $3.85 to $4.50, up 16.9%, and B300 from $7.85 to $9.50, up 21%. Its second increase in three months.
- October 7: AWS reserved Capacity Blocks moved to $5.970 per H100 accelerator-hour, the same rate across twelve regions.
- October 8: Nebius switched preemptible H100, H200, B200, B300 and RTX PRO 6000 to dynamic spot pricing. The published $2.15 became a floor of $0.79, with prices that can change every 15 minutes, including during a run, capped one cent below the on-demand rate.
- CoreWeave's HGX H100 node stayed at $49.24, or $6.16 per GPU.

Five things a headline rate doesn't tell you:

1. Per GPU or per node. CoreWeave, Oracle, Google and Azure sell H100s as 8-GPU nodes. If you need three, you pay for eight.
2. Volume rules. AWS charges $5.970 whether you take one GPU or eight. Lambda charges $4.29 for one and $3.99 each for eight.
3. Region. Nebius's H100 is in eu-north1 only. Google's 8-GPU H100 varies about 30% between its cheapest and priciest regions.
4. Purchase type. On-demand, spot, reserved and committed can differ by more than 3x on the same chip, with completely different reliability.
5. What's bundled. Lambda and CoreWeave list free egress. AWS charges about $0.09 per GB after an allowance.

The practical rule: compare the same purchase type, in the same region, at the same granularity, on the day you're buying. Anything else is comparing two different products.

results.title: AWS vs Azure vs GCP Cloud GPU Pricing [2026]
results.author: Sana Rahman
highlights:
# AWS vs Azure vs GCP Cloud GPU Pricing: B200 Up 15% [2026]

 Published October 23, 2026 · Updated November 2, 2026 

Sana Rahman

5,026 WORDS · UPDATED 2 WEEKS AGO

Cloud GPU pricing used to be a simple spreadsheet exercise: look up the hourly rate for an H100 instance, multiply by the hours you need, pick the cheapest provider. In October 2026 that spreadsheet broke. AWS raised its Blackwell B200 Capacity Block rate by roughly 15% on October 7, Microsoft Azure is one of the only major clouds still publishing a flat per-GPU hourly rate for H100 capacity, and Google Cloud has yet to post an official list price for H100, H200 or B200 instances at all. Comparing AWS vs Azure vs GCP cloud GPU pricing now means comparing three different billing philosophies, not just three price tags.

...

Microsoft Azure, by contrast, still publishes retail, pay-as-you-go rates for specific H100 virtual machine sizes. That transparency makes Azure the easiest provider to quote cleanly in a comparison article, which is exactly why most of the concrete numbers in this piece come from Azure’s own SKUs. Google Cloud sits at the opposite end: its A3 (H100), A3 Ultra (H200) and A4 (B200) instance families are confirmed to exist and to use those specific Nvidia GPUs, but no official Google Cloud page in the current research set states a public hourly price for any of them. Google increasingly routes customers toward Flex-start scheduling and committed-use contracts instead of a posted rate.

...

What AWS has not done, at least not in any officially confirmed source available as of October 23, 2026, is publish a flat on-demand hourly price for P5, P5e, P5en or P6-B200. Capacity Block pricing is explicitly dynamic, and AWS’s public materials direct buyers to request a quote or check the Capacity Blocks console rather than read a rate card.

...

Azure’s current GPU VM lineup for AI training includes NC40ads H100 v5, ND96isr H100 v5 and ND96isr H200 v5. Two of those SKUs give us the cleanest published numbers in this entire comparison. The NC40ads H100 v5 size, a single-H100 configuration, carried a reported East US pay-as-you-go Linux rate of $6.98 per hour as of October 19, 2026. The larger ND96isr H100 v5 size, which packs eight H100 GPUs, was reported at $98.32 per VM-hour in East US on the same date, which works out to $12.29 per GPU-hour.

Azure also lists an ND96isr H200 v5 size with eight H200 GPUs carrying 141 GB of memory each, making it the newest Hopper-class GPU family Azure has confirmed. Microsoft has not published an officially confirmed Azure B200 virtual machine family or hourly price as of October 23, 2026. Separately, Microsoft Foundry’s managed-compute tier, still in preview, bills hourly per accelerator across A100, H100, H200 and MI300 GPU families, but Microsoft’s documentation says rates vary by accelerator family, region, deployment scope and commitment term, and directs customers to the Azure Pricing Calculator rather than a published table.

...

Google Cloud confirmed on October 2, 2026 that its A3 instance family is powered by Nvidia H100 Tensor Core GPUs, while A3 Ultra instances carry Nvidia H200 Tensor Core GPUs. The newer A4 family, confirmed October 21, 2026, uses Nvidia HGX B200 GPUs, with the a4-highgpu-8g configuration packing eight B200 GPUs per instance. None of these three families has a confirmed, officially published public hourly price in the current research set. Google’s materials mention multiple consumption models for these instances, including on-demand, Spot and committed-use pricing, but do not spell out the specific rates for A3, A3 Ultra or A4.

Google also announced Confidential G4 instances on October 21, 2026, generally available with Nvidia RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell Server Edition GPUs across 36 zones through Compute Engine VMs and GKE nodes, and confirmed that Confidential Computing is now available on A4 instances through Nvidia HGX B200 paired with Intel TDX. On the same date, Google announced A5X bare-metal instances based on Nvidia’s newly unveiled Vera Rubin NVL72 platform, with general availability expected in November 2026. As of October 23, 2026, A5X is an announced, not-yet-available product, so it should not be treated as something customers can rent today.

...

## Cloud GPU Pricing Compared: What’s Published vs What’s a Black Box

This is the table that matters most for anyone trying to budget an AI training run, and it is deliberately conservative: it only includes rates that each provider has actually published, rather than third-party estimates.

| GPU | AWS (published rate) | Azure (published rate) | Google Cloud (published rate) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| H100, single GPU | No flat rate published; Capacity Blocks price dynamically | $6.98/hour, NC40ads H100 v5, East US, captured Oct. 19, 2026 | Not published |
| H100, 8-GPU node | No flat rate published | $98.32/hour ($12.29/GPU-hour), ND96isr H100 v5, East US, captured Oct. 19, 2026 | Not published |
| H200, 8-GPU node | No flat rate published | No flat on-demand VM rate confirmed in official sources | Not published |
| B200, per GPU-hour (Capacity Block) | $14.208/hour, effective Oct. 7, 2026, up from $12.355/hour (about a 15% increase) | Not offered / not confirmed | Not published; A4 uses Flex-start scheduling instead of a flat rate |

Independent GPU-rental trackers fill in some of the gaps, but their numbers are estimates rather than official list prices and should be read that way. GPU-pricing trackers reportedly placed AWS P5 H100 Capacity Block pricing around $5.97 per GPU-hour, effective October 7, 2026, and P5e/P5en H200 pricing between $6.87 and $7.895 per GPU-hour, effective October 7, 2026, though AWS itself does not publish those as fixed rates. Axis Intelligence’s October 22, 2026 comparison floated per-hour figures for Google Cloud H200 (A3 Ultra) and B200 (A4), but the same tracker found no confirmed on-demand price for those configurations, since they were marked as not available for direct purchase, so no official Google Cloud rate exists for either one. Treat any number below these published figures as directional until a provider confirms it on an official pricing page.

...

## The October 7 AWS B200 Price Hike, Explained

The single clearest pricing move any of the three providers made in the last three months was AWS’s. Effective October 7, 2026, AWS raised its P6-B200 Capacity Block price from $12.355 to $14.208 per accelerator-hour, an increase of approximately 15%, according to GPU-pricing trackers Axis Intelligence and Dev.to’s FastGPU column, which independently captured the same before-and-after figures. For an eight-GPU P6-B200 node, the current instance-hour rate is about $113.666, a noticeable jump in monthly spend for teams running sustained training jobs.

AWS frames Capacity Block pricing as dynamic by design, moving with supply and demand rather than sitting on a fixed card, so a mid-quarter increase is consistent with how the product is supposed to work. It is also a useful data point for the “which cloud is cheapest” question: it shows that even the provider with the most reservation flexibility, AWS, is not necessarily the cheapest or the most stable option for Blackwell-class capacity right now. Teams planning a long B200 training run in Q4 2026 should budget for the possibility of another adjustment before their reservation window closes, since trackers reported this was not the first GPU list-price increase AWS made in recent months.

...

Based strictly on what AWS, Microsoft and Google have confirmed as of October 23, 2026, Azure wins on transparency: it is the only provider of the three publishing a flat, dated per-GPU hourly rate for H100 capacity, at $6.98 per hour for a single GPU on NC40ads H100 v5 and $12.29 per GPU-hour for an eight-GPU ND96isr H100 v5 node. AWS wins on reservation flexibility and breadth, with Capacity Blocks able to lock in up to 512 H100 GPUs eight weeks ahead and the widest confirmed lineup across H100, H200, B200 and GB200, but that flexibility comes with dynamic pricing that just rose about 15% on its B200 tier. Google Cloud currently offers the least pricing transparency of the three for Nvidia-based instances, with no officially published rate for A3, A3 Ultra or A4, but it leads on confirmed confidential-computing availability and on its TPU 8i price-performance claim, and it has the earliest announced path to Nvidia’s next-generation Vera Rubin platform through A5X.

...

AWS’s P6-B200 Capacity Block price rose from $12.355 to $14.208 per accelerator-hour effective October 7, 2026, an increase of approximately 15%, according to GPU-pricing trackers Axis Intelligence and FastGPU, which captured matching before-and-after figures.

results.title: GPU Rental Price Report, November 2026 · EverXCloud
highlights:
GPU Rental Price Report, November 2026 · EverXCloud

# GPU Rental Price Report, November 2026

Public GPU-hour prices for H100, H200, B200, A100, L40S, RTX 4090 and RTX 5090 across 16 cloud providers, with medians and spreads.

## Executive summary

EverXCloud read the public pricing pages of 16 GPU cloud providers on 2026-10-26 and recorded 75 prices per GPU-hour for eight GPUs. On-demand prices for the same GPU still vary widely between providers, and spot, preemptible or community capacity costs far less than on-demand capacity.

This report covers third-party list prices only. Once the EverXCloud Marketplace launches, its own price index will be published from real transactions.

## Key findings

1. The median on-demand H100 SXM price across 11 providers is $3.99 per GPU-hour, from $3.14 to $6.16: the most expensive listing costs 2.0× the cheapest.
2. Spot, preemptible and community H100 SXM capacity has a median of $2.30 per GPU-hour across 3 providers, 42% below the on-demand median.
3. The H200 carries a 24% premium over the H100 SXM at the median ($4.94 vs $3.99 on demand, 10 providers).
4. On-demand B200 prices range from $6.00 to $8.60 per GPU-hour across 7 providers, with a median of $8.19.
5. The A100 80GB shows the widest relative spread among data center GPUs: 2.6× between the cheapest ($1.09) and the most expensive ($2.79) on-demand listing, across 9 providers.
6. AWS Capacity Blocks, a short-term reservation, list the H100 at $5.97 and the B200 at $14.21 per GPU-hour, 1.5× and 1.7× the on-demand medians of the other providers.

## Prices by GPU

...

## Methodology

- Prices were read on 2026-10-26 on each provider's official public pricing page, in USD per GPU-hour, excluding tax. No price was estimated, negotiated or taken from a third-party aggregator.
- One price per provider, GPU and offer type. When a provider lists several configurations for the same GPU, the lowest listed price was kept, and the listing is recorded in the data.
- Multi-GPU instances are converted to a per-GPU price by dividing the instance price by the number of GPUs (for example CoreWeave and AWS 8-GPU instances).
- On-demand and spot, preemptible or community prices are reported separately. AWS prices are Capacity Block rates, a short-term reservation, and are not included in the on-demand statistics.
- Providers whose pricing page could not be read, showed prices only after sign-in or on request, or did not map prices to GPUs unambiguously were left out: Vast.ai, Crusoe, Vultr, TensorDock, Fluidstack, Genesis Cloud, Google Cloud, Microsoft Azure, Voltage Park, Cudo Compute, Scaleway, Paperspace and SF Compute.
- The median of an even number of prices is the mean of the two middle values.

results.title: NVIDIA GPU Rental Rates Rise in 2026, Led by a 143% Jump for the H200 | Horizon Post
results.author: Layla Haddad
highlights:
The H200, launched in 2024, recorded the largest rental-rate increase in the figures reported by a16z. Behind its 143% gain were the B200 at 111%, the RTX PRO 6000 at 73% and the H100 at 54%. The A100, a 2020 model, rose 9%.

Ornn's October 23, 2026, Compute Price Index settlement put the B200 at $9.58 per GPU-hour and the H200 at $5.74. The H100 SXM settled at $3.17, followed by the RTX PRO 6000 at $1.54 and the A100 SXM4 at $1.09.

Those figures reflect completed rentals across the neocloud market, not advertised prices or quotes from individual providers. Ornn calculates the index once per trading day using volume-weighted, winsorized transaction averages.

An earlier snapshot shows how B200 rates had already been climbing. In an Ornn-based analysis published September 25, Data Gravity reported a rate of $8.01 per hour as of September 24, 2026, up 79% over three months.

...

The same report described price increases across several providers. AWS increased reserved GPU block rates by about 20% on July 1, 2026, while CoreWeave reportedly raised prices by about 25%. Nebius listed a B200 rate of $8.50 effective October 1, up from $7.15.

Oracle, meanwhile, renewed expiring GPU contracts at a 20% premium, according to the analysis, which reported that 97.9% of its AI capacity was in use.
